newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: focus - Germans spoil Bank Austria selloff party.
newsitem.headline: focus - Germans spoil Bank Austria selloff party.

text.p: Austrian politicians delivered a stinging rebuke to Bank Austria's majority owners on Monday following revelations that Germany's WestLB had secured an option to take control of the nation's top bank.
The news threatened to derail Vienna City's plans to sell its indirect 49 percent voting stake in Bank Austria over the next six years without sacrificing a majority Austrian interest.
"What were those involved in the negotiations with WestLB thinking of?" asked conservative Othmar Karas, general secretary of the People's Party.
"It is a scandal that there was no public debate and we were not informed," added Karas, whose party rules in coalition with Chancellor Viktor Klima's Social Democrats.
Westdeutsche Landesbank Girozentrale confirmed it had gained first refusal on the shares at the end of 1995 when it acquired a 10.7 percent voting stake in Bank Austria.
"We have an option to buy the shares but we have nothing to add to that," said WestLB spokesman Michael Wilde.
The deal with WestLB was negotiated by Vienna city holding company AVZ -- whose board is chaired by Bank Austria chief executive Gerhard Randa and includes several Social Democrat politicians.

AVZ controls 45.15 percent of Bank Austria voting stock, or 39.93 percent of share capital. A second holding company, Wiener Holding, has Vienna's remaining four percent of voting stock, representing 3.53 percent of share capital.
"Vienna Council's proposal to privatise Bank Austria is not worth the paper it is written on," criticised Thomas Prinzhorn, economy spokesman for the opposition Freedom Party.
"The WestLB deal only serves to prove how highly politicised the entire Austrian banking sector is," he added, referring to the six years it took the state to withdraw from Creditanstalt .
Creditanstalt was finally sold to Bank Austria in January.

Bank Austria, which has made no secret of its opposition to Vienna Council's privatisation plan, said only AVZ had a legal right to offload its shares. Vienna politicians insist the city can act alone since it guarantees all AVZ liabilities.

The row has erupted at an awkward time for Bank Austria, which is preparing for a three billion schillings ($250 million) capital increase this summer and may have to contend with the sale of the state's 17 percent stake before the end of the year.
On Monday Bank Austria preferred shares closed one schilling up at 421.
Bank Austria spokesman Heimo Hackl defended the WestLB deal and insisted there was no attempt to keep the details secret.
"The AVZ board gave its unanimous approval in December 1995," he said, adding that the decision was made public. ($ = 12.05 Austrian Schillings)
